subject: use of a random effect in a binomial mixed effects model

messages.author: 7cae77e58c6f814b
messages.subject: use of a random effect in a binomial mixed effects model
parts:
Hello all:

I am trying to fit a seemingly simple GLM through WinBUGS but am having trouble wrapping my head around the appropriate model structure. 

I have 90 data sets collected by independent researchers on a variety of fish species (30 species total).  Each data set contains numbers of individuals experiencing mortality and also numbers studied.  So, the response data are binomially distributed.  There are multiple data sets for some species but just one data set for other species.  It makes sense for me to consider species as a random effect in either a random intercepts or a random coefficients model, as laid out in Kery’s Introduction to WinBUGS Chapter 12 (but using the logit link for the binomially distributed response data: chapter 19).  Considering species as a random effect makes sense given the usual arguments for a random effect and given that the same species is common to some of the 90 data sets.

I would like to determine whether each of two factors is a meaningful covariate of the response data.  One factor is categorical (what type of collection gear the researcher used, call it H), with two levels.  The other factor is continuous (a life history trait, call it K).  However, for this continuous factor K, there is only one value for species.  Put another way, for each species, there is no contrast in a trait that may nonetheless covary with the response.   

For a random coefficients model, it doesn’t make sense for me to have a likelihood such as

for (I in 1:n) {

C[i] ~dbin(p[i], N[i])

logit(p[i]) <- alpha[species[i]] + beta1[species[i]]*K[i] + beta2*H[i]

}

because, again, there is only 1 value of K per species.   Eliminating K from the model would be eliminating a factor that might explain the response data.  In contrast, retaining K in the model while getting rid of the species indicator also does not seem to make sense due to lack of contrast in the K data for each species, and due to the fact that there are multiple data sets for some species.

Thank you for any suggestions or ideas on appropriate model structures to consider.

Paul Rudershausen

messages.subject: Re: use of a random effect in a binomial mixed effects model
parts:
Hi,

Perhaps you should consider the example of site-occupancy modeling for multiple species. 
If I understand you well, I think you need 1) a loop that passes through 1: S species to estimate the species-specific e.g. p, and then 2) create a vector with 1:S species to relate with the trait K.

Cheers,
André
